name: Outside Heel Hook from Outside Ashi-Garami
description: Master the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami with complete finishing mechanics, defensive strategies, and safety protocols for leg lock practitioners.
summary: The outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami is a rotational knee submission that twists the trapped heel laterally from a figure-four entanglement, attacking the ACL and LCL to produce one of no-gi grappling's highest-percentage leg-lock finishes.
target_area: Knee joint, ankle joint, and surrounding ligaments
overview:
From the outside ashi-garami entanglement, the attacker's figure-four leg configuration naturally isolates the opponent's leg while their perpendicular body alignment creates rotational leverage against the knee joint. The outside angle provides direct access to the heel, making this a mechanically efficient finishing position that rewards technical precision over raw strength. Because the finish is available directly from a foundational entanglement rather than requiring advancement to saddle or inside ashi first, it sees heavy use across no-gi and submission-only competition.

The attacker cups the opponent's heel with both hands in a figure-four or butterfly grip, then applies controlled rotational force by turning the heel laterally while extending their hips. Because outside ashi-garami attacks from an outside angle, the rotation targets the lateral collateral ligament complex and can compromise the anterior cruciate ligament. This makes the technique exceptionally dangerous and demands strict adherence to safety protocols during training.

Unlike finishing from saddle or inside ashi where both legs are controlled, outside ashi-garami leaves the opponent's far leg free, creating viable escape routes. The attacker must balance maintaining the leg triangle with committing their upper body to the heel hook grip. This tension between control and attack makes timing critical and distinguishes the technique from more dominant finishing positions where positional security allows deliberate finishing attempts.

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW - minimum 5-7 seconds progressive pressure in training, NEVER sudden rotation
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on partner or mat
Physical foot tap with free leg
release_protocol: Immediately release rotational pressure on heel
Release the figure-four grip or heel cup
Allow opponent to straighten leg naturally
training_restrictions: NEVER apply sudden rotational force - always slow and progressive
NEVER practice at competition speed during training
NEVER continue past first sign of discomfort
Only train with experienced partners who understand leg locks
Always ensure clear communication before training leg locks
Tap early and often - do not test flexibility limits
Prohibited for white and blue belts in most IBJJF competitions
Never practice on injured knees or with prior knee injuries without medical clearance

variations_and_setups.description: Classical outside heel hook using a figure-four grip with the near-side hand cupping the heel and the far-side hand threading under to lock. Hip extension drives the breaking pressure while upper body rotation targets the lateral knee structures.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have clean heel access and your opponent has not yet established a boot defense or begun rolling

variations_and_setups.description: Both hands interlace fingers around the heel in a butterfly configuration rather than figure-four. Provides stronger rotational control and is harder to strip but requires both hands to commit simultaneously.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is actively grip-fighting and you need maximum grip security before committing to the finish

variations_and_setups.description: Rather than rotating with arms, pull the heel tight to your chest and use your entire torso rotation to apply breaking pressure. This variation generates more torque with less arm fatigue.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against larger opponents or when your arm grip is fatiguing during an extended finishing sequence

attacker.name: from Outside Ashi-Garami Attacker
attacker.description: Complete attacking guide for the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami covering grip mechanics, hip extension, rotational finishing, and safety protocols.
attacker.overview: Attacking the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami requires establishing proper heel access while maintaining the figure-four leg triangle configuration. The attacker must manage the tension between maintaining positional control through their legs and committing their upper body to the heel hook grip. Success depends on proper sequencing: secure the heel cup, establish rotational control, extend the hips to create breaking pressure, and apply slow controlled rotation. The outside angle provides natural leverage against the lateral knee structures, but the opponent's free far leg creates escape opportunities that demand precise timing. The finish is most effective when the opponent is occupied defending position rather than actively working leg extraction.
key_principles: Secure heel access before committing to the finish - premature rotation without proper grip wastes the attempt and alerts the opponent
Maintain tight figure-four leg configuration throughout the finishing sequence to prevent leg extraction during the submission attempt
Use hip extension as the primary breaking mechanism rather than arm strength alone - your hips generate far more force than your arms
Control opponent's hip rotation with your legs to prevent them from turning with the rotational force and neutralizing the submission
Apply rotation progressively over 5-7 seconds minimum - the heel hook requires slow controlled torque, not explosive twisting
Keep elbows clamped tight to your ribcage to maximize rotational leverage and prevent grip strips
Time the finish when opponent is defending positionally rather than actively scrambling to extract their leg
setup_requirements: Established outside ashi-garami with tight figure-four leg triangle eliminating all space between your legs and opponent's trapped leg
Heel access confirmed - opponent's heel is exposed and reachable, not hidden behind their opposite knee or tucked against their body
Perpendicular or diagonal hip angle (45-90 degrees) to opponent's leg line, torso facing toward their trapped leg
Control of opponent's hip rotation through leg pressure preventing them from externally rotating their knee
Opponent's far leg managed - either controlled with your body positioning or neutralized through timing

execution_steps.description: Cup the opponent's heel with your near-side hand, wrapping your fingers around the Achilles tendon area with your wrist bone positioned firmly against the heel bone itself. Your palm faces upward and your grip locks around the heel like a cup, not the toes or mid-foot. This initial grip determines the quality of the entire finish.

Thread your far-side hand under your near-side forearm to create a figure-four grip configuration that locks the heel in place. Your far-side hand grips your own wrist or forearm, creating a closed loop around the opponent's heel that they cannot easily strip. Ensure no slack exists in the grip structure.

Pull both elbows tight against your ribcage to eliminate any gap between your arms and body. This connects the heel hook grip to your core, ensuring that torso rotation translates directly into rotational pressure on the heel. Loose elbows allow the opponent to create space and strip the grip before the finish.

Squeeze your figure-four leg configuration by pulling your inside foot back toward your buttocks and pressing your outside leg down across their thigh. This eliminates the last remaining space and prevents the opponent from extracting their leg during the finishing sequence. The legs provide the positional anchor while your upper body executes the submission.

Drive your hips forward toward the opponent's trapped leg, creating extension pressure that straightens their leg against your body. This hip extension is the primary power source for the heel hook - it locks their leg in a straight line that cannot absorb rotational force. Without hip extension, the submission lacks the structural pressure needed to finish.

While maintaining hip extension, rotate the heel laterally toward the outside of the opponent's knee using your entire upper body, not just your arms. The rotation should be slow, progressive, and controlled over a minimum of 5-7 seconds in training. Feel for the breaking point and stop immediately upon tap. The lateral rotation attacks the LCL and ACL simultaneously.

common_counters.counter: Boot defense - opponent hides heel by tucking foot behind opposite knee or turning toes inward
common_counters.your_response: Use your outside hand to strip their defensive grip or peel their foot free, angle your hips to create heel exposure, or transition to a straight ankle lock which does not require heel access

common_counters.counter: Leg straightening and extraction - opponent fights to straighten their leg and pull it free from the figure-four
common_counters.your_response: Maintain constant clamp pressure with your legs, use hip extension to prevent full straightening, and accelerate your finishing sequence before extraction completes

common_counters.counter: Rolling with the rotation - opponent rolls their entire body in the direction of the heel hook rotation to relieve pressure
common_counters.your_response: Follow their roll while maintaining grip and leg configuration, the rotation still creates ligament stress even when they roll, or transition to inside ashi as their roll exposes the far leg

common_counters.counter: Standing posture escape - opponent posts on free leg and drives upward to create height advantage and extraction angle
common_counters.your_response: If they begin standing before you have heel access, immediately tighten legs and sweep their posting leg or transition to a kneebar on the trapped leg before they achieve full standing

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish with arm strength alone rather than hip extension
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient torque to finish the submission, rapid grip fatigue, and the opponent can defend with minimal effort since arm rotation lacks power
common_errors.correction: Use hip extension as the primary breaking mechanism by driving hips forward to straighten the opponent's leg, then rotate with your entire torso connected to the grip through clamped elbows

common_errors.error: Loose leg triangle during the finishing attempt
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their leg mid-submission, wasting the grip and position while potentially ending up in a worse entanglement for the attacker
common_errors.correction: Squeeze your figure-four leg configuration tight before committing to the heel grip, pull inside foot toward buttocks, and maintain leg pressure throughout the entire finishing sequence

common_errors.error: Explosive rotation instead of progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Serious risk of knee injury to training partner due to the speed at which heel hooks cause damage, and the explosive motion telegraphs the finish allowing experienced opponents to defend
common_errors.correction: Apply slow steady rotation over a minimum of 5-7 seconds in training, feel for resistance gradually increasing, and stop immediately upon any tap signal

common_errors.error: Gripping too high on the foot instead of cupping the heel bone
common_errors.consequence: Reduced rotational leverage because the fulcrum point is wrong, opponent can kick their foot free more easily, and the submission pressure disperses rather than concentrating on knee ligaments
common_errors.correction: Position your wrist bone directly against the heel bone with fingers wrapping the Achilles tendon, ensuring the grip cups the heel itself rather than the toes, arch, or mid-foot

common_errors.error: Neglecting perpendicular hip angle before initiating the finish
common_errors.consequence: Suboptimal leverage makes the finish significantly harder, reduces the mechanical advantage of the outside angle, and allows the opponent more room to rotate and escape
common_errors.correction: Establish a 45-90 degree angle between your torso and the opponent's leg line before securing the heel grip, adjust hip position to face directly toward their trapped leg

common_errors.error: Releasing leg pressure when reaching for the heel
common_errors.consequence: Creates a window for the opponent to extract their leg as your positional control decreases at the exact moment you commit to the submission grip
common_errors.correction: Maintain or increase leg squeeze as you reach for the heel, practice the transition from positional legs to attacking grip without any release of leg pressure

training_progressions.focus: Heel cup positioning and figure-four grip
training_progressions.description: Practice securing the heel cup and figure-four grip on a stationary partner with no resistance. Focus on wrist bone placement against the heel, finger positioning around the Achilles, and eliminating slack in the grip structure. 20 repetitions each side.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Hip extension and rotation mechanics
training_progressions.focus: Connecting hip drive to rotational finish
training_progressions.description: From established outside ashi with grip secured, practice the hip extension to rotation sequence at extremely slow speed with zero resistance. Partner provides verbal feedback on pressure buildup. Focus on elbows-to-ribs connection and torso-driven rotation rather than arm torque.

Partner provides 25%, then 50%, then 75% resistance using boot defense, leg straightening, and rolling counters. Practice maintaining grip and adjusting finishing mechanics against each defense. Tap early and frequently. 5-minute rounds per resistance level.

training_progressions.focus: Complete sequence from position to finish
training_progressions.description: Start in established outside ashi-garami, both partners work live with full resistance. Attacker works to secure heel and finish, defender works to escape or defend. 3-minute rounds with reset on escape or submission. Emphasize slow controlled rotation even under competitive pressure.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 5: Chain attacks from failed finish
training_progressions.focus: Transitioning when heel hook is defended
training_progressions.description: Practice flowing from a defended outside heel hook into alternative attacks: transition to inside ashi for inside heel hook, switch to straight ankle lock, or advance to saddle. Develop the ability to recognize which alternative is available based on the opponent's defensive response.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The outside heel hook primarily attacks the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of the knee joint through lateral rotational force. The rotation also stresses the meniscus and can compromise the medial collateral ligament (MCL) and posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) depending on the angle of application. The ankle ligaments experience secondary stress from the rotational torque transmitted through the lower leg.

flashcards.question: What is the primary power source for finishing the outside heel hook and why?
flashcards.answer: Hip extension is the primary power source for finishing the outside heel hook. Driving the hips forward straightens the opponent's leg against your body, creating a rigid structure that cannot absorb rotational force. Without hip extension, the opponent's bent leg can flex and rotate with your grip, dissipating the submission pressure. Your arms guide the direction of rotation while your hips generate the structural pressure that makes the rotation effective against the knee ligaments.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins hiding their heel behind their opposite knee - what adjustments prevent this defense from succeeding?
flashcards.answer: Use your outside hand to peel their defensive foot away from the knee, or angle your hips further toward their trapped leg to create a line of access around their boot defense. If the boot is fully locked, consider transitioning to a straight ankle lock which does not require heel access, or use your far-side hand to control their defensive leg at the knee to prevent the tuck. You can also elevate your hips to change the angle and expose the heel from underneath their defense.

flashcards.question: At what point during the finishing sequence does the opponent lose the ability to safely defend?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when hip extension has straightened the leg and rotational pressure has engaged the ligaments beyond their neutral range. Before this point, the opponent can boot defend, straighten and extract, or roll with the rotation. Once the heel is cupped with a locked figure-four grip, elbows are clamped, and hip extension has created a rigid straight-leg structure, the defender's only safe option is to tap immediately. This is why progressive application speed is critical in training.

flashcards.question: Why must rotation be applied progressively over 5-7 seconds minimum during training?
flashcards.answer: Heel hooks cause ligament damage at speeds faster than the human nervous system can register pain. Unlike joint locks where increasing pain provides a clear warning signal before structural damage, the heel hook can tear ligaments before the defender feels significant discomfort. Progressive 5-7 second rotation gives the defender time to recognize pressure buildup and tap before structural damage occurs. Explosive rotation in training creates unacceptable injury risk because the damage occurs before any tap signal is possible.

flashcards.question: How should you adjust your grip if the opponent's foot is sweaty and your initial heel cup is slipping?
flashcards.answer: Switch from a standard heel cup to a butterfly grip where both hands interlace fingers around the heel, providing stronger friction and a closed-loop grip that is harder to slip. You can also pull the heel tighter to your chest to use your torso as additional friction surface. Wipe your hands on your shorts if possible before re-gripping. Avoid gripping harder with just your fingers as this accelerates fatigue without improving security. The chest-to-foot finishing variation is specifically designed for slippery conditions.

flashcards.question: What common finishing error explains why many practitioners fail to finish despite having a seemingly good grip?
flashcards.answer: The most common reason is attempting to finish with arm rotation alone without establishing hip extension first. When the opponent's leg remains bent, it can absorb and redirect rotational force by flexing at the knee. The arms alone generate insufficient torque to overcome a bent knee's resistance. The correction is to drive hips forward to straighten the leg completely before initiating rotation, creating a rigid lever that transmits all rotational force directly to the knee ligaments.

flashcards.question: How does the outside heel hook finish differ in competition versus training application?
flashcards.answer: In competition, practitioners may apply the heel hook faster and with more commitment since the stakes of losing the grip are higher. However, responsible competitors still apply progressively rather than explosively. In training, the minimum 5-7 second application window is mandatory, and both partners should communicate clearly before engaging in heel hook exchanges. The mechanical technique is identical, but training demands more deliberate speed control, earlier tapping, and verbal communication about pressure levels throughout the attempt.

flashcards.question: What is the correct release protocol after your opponent taps to the outside heel hook?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all rotational pressure on the heel first, then release the figure-four grip, followed by removing hip extension pressure. Allow the opponent to straighten their leg naturally without forcing any movement. Never apply rotation while releasing as this can cause damage during the release itself. Check your partner's condition before continuing the round. The release sequence prioritizes removing rotational force first because that is the primary injury mechanism.

flashcards.question: Your opponent is rolling with your rotation to relieve pressure - should you chase the roll or transition?
flashcards.answer: Evaluate whether the roll is truly relieving pressure or just repositioning. If your grip is secure and elbows remain clamped, follow the roll while maintaining your grip because the rotational force on the knee ligaments persists even as the body rotates. If the roll creates enough slack for them to begin extracting their leg, transition to inside ashi by threading your leg through as their rotation exposes the far side, giving you a higher-percentage inside heel hook opportunity.

defender.name: from Outside Ashi-Garami Defender
defender.description: Complete defensive guide against the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami covering recognition, escape timing, boot defense, and safe tapping protocols.
defender.overview: Defending the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami requires immediate recognition and prioritized defensive responses executed in the correct sequence. The defender must first protect their heel from being accessed by the attacker, then prevent rotational control from being established, and finally work systematic escape sequences that address both the leg entanglement and the submission grip. Defense before the heel is cupped is dramatically more effective than defense after rotation begins, making early recognition the single most important defensive skill. Once rotation engages the knee ligaments, the only safe response is an immediate tap - there is no reliable late-stage escape from a locked outside heel hook.
key_principles: Defend the heel first and foremost - hide it behind your opposite knee or tuck it against your body before the attacker can establish a grip
Tap immediately once rotational pressure engages your knee ligaments - there is no safe late-stage escape from a locked heel hook
Maintain standing or elevated posture whenever possible as height advantage limits the attacker's leverage and creates extraction angles
Fight grips before they lock - stripping a partially established heel cup is far easier than breaking a locked figure-four
Use internal hip rotation to protect the knee from lateral rotational force that attacks the ligaments
Stay calm and work methodically through escape sequences rather than panicking and making explosive movements that expose the heel
Recognize the submission attempt early by monitoring the attacker's hand positioning and body angle changes
recognition_cues: Attacker's near-side hand moving toward your heel or Achilles area while you are trapped in their outside ashi-garami
Attacker's upper body rotating to face your trapped leg, establishing the perpendicular angle needed for finishing mechanics
Feeling increased hip extension pressure as attacker drives hips forward to straighten your trapped leg
Attacker's elbows clamping tight to their ribcage after securing a grip on your foot, indicating commitment to the finish
Attacker's far-side hand threading under their near-side forearm to establish the figure-four lock around your heel

defensive_options.action: Boot defense - hide heel behind opposite knee or tuck foot inward to deny heel access
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you recognize the attacker reaching for your heel, before any grip is established on the foot
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker cannot establish heel cup grip and must either work to strip your boot defense or abandon the heel hook attempt
defensive_options.risk: May expose your far leg to alternative attacks if you over-commit to the boot, and does not address the underlying leg entanglement

defensive_options.action: Grip strip and leg extraction - fight the heel cup grip while straightening leg to pull free from figure-four
defensive_options.when_to_use: When attacker has partial but not fully locked grip on your heel, and their leg triangle has some looseness
defensive_options.if_successful: Complete escape from leg entanglement returning to neutral or advantageous position
defensive_options.risk: If the leg triangle tightens during extraction attempt, you may accelerate the submission by straightening into their extension pressure

defensive_options.action: Roll with rotation and counter-entangle - roll in the direction of the heel hook rotation while establishing your own leg control
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has established grip and begun rotation, as a last resort before tapping
defensive_options.if_successful: Reduces rotational pressure on knee and may create a scramble or mutual leg entanglement situation
defensive_options.risk: If rotation has already engaged the ligaments significantly, rolling may not relieve enough pressure and you should tap instead

defensive_options.action: Standing posture escape - post on free leg and drive upward to create height advantage and extraction angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker's leg triangle is loose enough to allow upward movement and before heel grip is established
defensive_options.if_successful: Height advantage makes leg extraction significantly easier and limits attacker's leverage for finishing
defensive_options.risk: If attacker sweeps your posting leg or transitions to kneebar, you may end up in a worse position than the original entanglement

escape_paths: Boot defense to heel hide, followed by standing posture and leg extraction through internal hip rotation while controlling the attacker's gripping hand
Grip strip on partially established heel cup, immediate leg straightening and extraction before the attacker can re-establish the figure-four lock
Counter-entangle by establishing your own leg control on the attacker's exposed leg while rolling to neutralize rotational pressure

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the heel hook grip and extract your leg from the entanglement by straightening your leg and using internal hip rotation while the attacker's leg triangle is loosened from their commitment to the finishing grip
Successfully boot defend to deny heel access, then work systematic leg extraction that returns you to a neutral leg entanglement where neither player has a submission grip established

common_errors.error: Allowing the heel to become exposed while focusing on other aspects of the defense
common_errors.consequence: Attacker secures heel cup grip and can immediately begin the finishing sequence, dramatically reducing your defensive options to tapping only
common_errors.correction: Prioritize heel protection above all other defensive actions - hide the heel behind your opposite knee or tuck it against your body before addressing the leg entanglement

common_errors.error: Attempting to power out of the submission by straightening the leg after rotation has begun
common_errors.consequence: Straightening the leg into the attacker's hip extension creates a rigid lever that amplifies rotational force on the knee ligaments, potentially causing immediate injury
common_errors.correction: Once rotation has engaged, tap immediately rather than trying to straighten and extract - there is no reliable muscular defense against a locked heel hook under rotation

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive jerking movements to escape
common_errors.consequence: Explosive movement can expose the heel, tighten the attacker's leg triangle, or create sudden rotational force on your own knee ligaments
common_errors.correction: Remain calm and work methodically through defensive sequences - breathe deeply, assess heel status, identify grip security, then execute the appropriate defense

common_errors.error: Delaying the tap when rotation pressure is felt on the knee
common_errors.consequence: Heel hooks cause ligament damage faster than pain signals register, meaning by the time you feel significant pain the structural damage may already be done
common_errors.correction: Tap at the first sign of rotational pressure on the knee, not when pain becomes significant - develop the habit of early tapping in training to protect long-term joint health

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that an outside heel hook is being set up from outside ashi-garami?
flashcards.answer: Watch for the attacker's near-side hand moving toward your heel or Achilles area, their upper body rotating to face your trapped leg at a perpendicular angle, increased hip extension pressure straightening your leg, and their elbows clamping tight to their ribcage after gripping your foot. The far-side hand threading under the near-side forearm to establish a figure-four confirms the finishing attempt has begun.

flashcards.question: When is the correct time to tap to an outside heel hook and why is early tapping critical?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately at the first sensation of rotational pressure on your knee joint. Unlike other submissions where increasing pain provides a gradual warning before structural damage, heel hooks can tear knee ligaments faster than the nervous system can register pain. By the time you feel significant pain, the ACL or other ligaments may already be compromised. Develop the habit of tapping as soon as you feel rotational engagement on the knee, not when pain becomes severe.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the outside heel hook from outside ashi-garami?
flashcards.answer: The primary defense is the boot defense, hiding your heel behind your opposite knee before the attacker can grip it. If they have a partial grip, strip it while straightening your leg to extract from the entanglement. If they have begun rotation, you can attempt to roll with the direction of rotation to reduce pressure, but if significant rotational force is engaged, the only safe option is an immediate tap. Standing posture escape works when the leg triangle is loose enough to allow upward movement.

flashcards.question: Why is straightening your leg after rotation has begun a dangerous defensive error?
flashcards.answer: Straightening your leg into the attacker's hip extension creates a rigid lever that amplifies rotational force on the knee ligaments rather than relieving it. A bent knee can absorb some rotational force through flexion, but a straight knee transmits all rotation directly to the ligament structures. This is why hip extension is the attacker's primary finishing mechanism and why defenders should avoid straightening into it once rotation is engaged.

flashcards.question: Your boot defense has been stripped and the attacker is reaching for your heel - what immediate action should you take?
flashcards.answer: Immediately attempt to re-establish the boot defense by pulling your heel back behind your opposite knee or tucking it against your body. Simultaneously use your hands to grip-fight against the attacker's reaching hand, focusing on controlling their wrist to prevent the heel cup from being established. If you cannot re-hide the heel, begin straightening your leg for extraction before the figure-four grip locks. If the grip locks with your heel cupped, prepare to tap early once any rotational pressure begins.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying submission setup cues and developing early tap habits
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes outside ashi-garami and slowly progresses through the heel hook setup. Practice identifying each stage: hand movement toward heel, grip establishment, hip extension, rotation initiation. Tap at the first sign of rotational engagement on the knee. 20 repetitions focusing purely on recognition and tap timing.

Partner reaches for your heel at progressively faster speeds. Practice tucking the heel behind the opposite knee and maintaining the boot defense under pressure. Develop the reflex to protect the heel immediately when the attacker's hands move toward your foot. 10-minute rounds at 25%, 50%, then 75% speed.

training_progressions.focus: Breaking partial grips and extracting the trapped leg
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes partial heel cup grip at various stages of completion. Practice stripping the grip using wrist control and hand fighting while simultaneously working leg extraction through straightening and internal hip rotation. Reset after each escape attempt.

training_progressions.focus: Full defensive sequence against live attacks
training_progressions.description: Start in outside ashi-garami with attacker working live toward the heel hook. Defender practices full defensive sequences including boot defense, grip fighting, extraction attempts, and rolling escapes. Emphasis on early tapping when rotation engages. 3-minute rounds with full resistance.
